comment.value: This paper presents a large scale benchmark for video frame interpolation, which is a clear contribution to the community.  After the rebuttal and discussion the paper received an accept and two marginally above accepts. The three reviewers agree that the dataset is of high quality, diverse, includes a solid comparison with a previous dataset, and video examples, and that the paper should be accepted.
The rebuttal addresses some of my concerns, I'm willing to raise the score.

Thank you very much for your review. Improvements based on the suggestions are listed below.

> 1. More videos in other domains such as anime or 3D rendering would significantly increase the usefulness of this dataset 

The further inclusion of videos from other domains is indeed a promising direction for extending the dataset further. The motivation for using natural scenes is similar to the rest of the widely-used VFI datasets [6,32,35,38,51,56,57,64] as they include large variations in terms of video conditions. LAVIB also includes 2,438 videos from misc domains such as video game captures and graphics demos which are more than previous datasets and benchmarks [47,h].


Refs.

[h] 1. Vatolin D (online) Available from: https://videoprocessing.ai/benchmarks/video-frame-interpolation.html 


> 2. Documentation on intended use, maintenance, and availability

Thank you. This will be added to the text. The benchmark code is made publicly available on GitHub ([link](https://github.com/alexandrosstergiou/LAVIB)) and will be maintained for subsequent iterations. The full dataset is also publicly available on HuggingFace ([link](https://huggingface.co/datasets/astergiou/LAVIB/tree/main)).

rebuttal.value:
Thank you for your review and the suggested improvements. Please find below clarifications/updates based on the points raised.

> 1. 283K video clips may not fully justify the large-scale claim

In comparison to the previously largest VFI dataset [64], LAVIB contains $\times3$ more videos with the total dataset duration also being $\times13$ larger. The term "large-scale" refers explicitly to the domain of VFI for which LAVIB aims to provide a benchmark suite based on high-resolution videos for a diverse set of challenges. This is a stepping stone towards enabling future works to further increase scale. This domain-specific distinction of "large-scale" will be made clearer in the text.     


> 2. Minimize bias based on the search terms used

(Answered jointly in the main rebuttal)

> 3. Exploring the impact of other crucial factors such as resolution and frame rate.

Certainly agree. Both frame rate and resolution are also important factors to the performance of VFI methods. The focus on motion, frame sharpness, video contrast, and luminance is primarily for the data collection and definition of challenges. The use of these statics stems from their usefulness in capturing *scene attributes*. As resolution and frame rate relate more to *processing settings* such as the input size and sampling rate they can be best explored in ablations: 


- __Frame rate__: Table 8 compares the performance of a LAVIB- and Vimeo90K-trained models over triplets and septuplets across temporal resolutions. As shown, the LAVIB-trained model can maintain reasonable performance even in the significantly more challenging schemes of $\times 3$ ($20 \rightarrow 60\text{fps}$) and $\times 4$ ($15 \rightarrow 60\text{fps}$) interpolation compared to the baseline trained with [64]. LAVIB's standardized 60fps also enables future works to explore VFI over multiple temporal resolutions. Supplementary to Tab. 8, Tab. X6 reports performance on 30fps targets created by sampling every 2 frames to form triplets.



- __Frame resolution__: Following [15,22,67], models are trained with $ 256 \times 256 $ frame resolution. Tables X4 and X5 include ablations on frame sizes. Overall, a small decrease in performance is observed when training on lower resolutions. However, this drop is more evident when training on the smaller and less diverse Vimeo-90K. The large and diverse LAVIB training set can therefore also be an effective alternative for training on lower compute resources in which full-resolution videos do not fit in memory.  



> 4. Providing video results

Thank you for this suggestion. Video examples are now available on the project page ([link](https://alexandrosstergiou.github.io/datasets/LAVIB/index.html)) for each OOD challenge. The videos are made by combining the interpolated frames from all sequential triplets in the video. A slider is also added to switch between the interpolated frames and ground truth.

rebuttal.value:
Thank you for your review. Clarifications and improvements to address the pointed weaknesses are detailed below.

> 1. Detail ways of mitigating computational costs of running experiments.

Thank you for this suggestion. The training computational costs of VFI methods have only been sparsely explored up to this point as the sizes of previous datasets have been limited. A discussion on potential avenues of efficiency improvements can encourage future works. Based on other video understanding tasks, frame-level quantization [a,b], knowledge distillation [c,d], and salient frame sampling [e,f,g] can be imported and adapted to improve training efficiency. A discussion will be added in the updated version to overview efficiency-based outlooks for VFI.

Refs.

[a] Sun, X. et al. Dynamic network quantization for efficient video inference. ICCV 2021.

[b] Abati, D., et al. ResQ: Residual Quantization for Video Perception. ICCV 2023.

[c] Ma, C., et al. Rethinking resolution in the context of efficient video recognition. NeurIPS 2022.

[d] Kim, H., et al., 2021. Efficient action recognition via dynamic knowledge propagation. ICCV 2021.

[e] Wu, Z., et al., Adaframe: Adaptive frame selection for fast video recognition. CVPR 2019.

[f] Xia, B., et al. Nsnet: Non-saliency suppression sampler for efficient video recognition. ECCV 2022.

[g] Wang, Y., et al., Adafocusv3: On unified spatial-temporal dynamic video recognition. ECCV 2022.



> 2. Exploring biases based on the web-based collection.

(Answered jointly in the main rebuttal)

> 3. Detailed explanation of how the metrics are used for the collection.

From the dense-coarse sampling detailed in L157-169, a total of 17,204 10-second 4K clips are collected. Two segmentation stages are then performed.
- __Temporal segment selection__ is based on the average flow magnitude. All available temporal 1sec crops are initially considered. Using FlowFormer [14], the 1sec clips of the 20\% highest space-time average motion magnitude are selected.
- __Spatial segment selection__ uses all four statistics. Four tubelets are created by dividing video frames with a 2x2 grid. ALV, ARL, ARMS, and AFM are computed per tubelet. Tubelets with the 80\% lowest or highest combined ALV, ARL, ARMS, and AFM, statistics are selected to compile LAVIB.

The complete pipeline is shown in Fig. 2. The statistics are also used to create the splits detailed in L183-182 and in A2 at the appendix. 

To improve clarity, the temporal and spatial segment selection paragraphs in L120-L182 will be updated. To make the correspondence between video attributes and the metrics detailed in $\S 3$ more explicit, the paragraph headers will be adjusted.

rebuttal.value:
Many thanks to the reviewers for their time and effort. Their positive comments on the writing quality, thorough benchmarking, and overall value of the dataset are highly appreciated. A shared comment from R-E9PZ and R-WSo6 was the need for an in-depth discussion on the vocabulary used for data collection. This is answered collectively below. Responses, clarifications, and enhancements based on the rest of the comments are provided in individual rebuttals. A PDF with the figures and tables referenced is also provided.   


> The paper does not thoroughly discuss biases in the data collection.

Thanks to the reviewers for this point. Videos are sourced by a vocabulary with primarily location and action-based queries. Other sources such as screen recordings, generated demos, time lapses, or HDR footage are also included; e.g. using misc terms, on a smaller scale (\~7% of videos). This is due to statistics such as sharpness (ALV) and luminance (ARL) being optimized in such videos -- thus containing only small variations. The narrow ALV/ARL distributions of videos sourced from misc queries are compared to an equally sized random sample from LAVIB in Fig. X1. Further distribution graphs for all terms are shown in Figs. X2 and X3, which will be included in the updated version alongside graphs for AFM and ARMS.

The following paragraphs further discuss potential biases and remedies for each vocabulary term, and will also be added to the paper.


### Location

- __Motivation__. Natural scenes were found to have a large number of 4K footage from diverse camera types with minimal edits. Using an exhaustive list of locations is not feasible given the search space.

- __Remedy used__. Instead, a list of locations was manually created based on the number of returned videos per location. Oversaturation of similar video locations; e.g. same country, was also manually adjusted for the selected terms.

- __Limitations__. This does result in some selectivity. However, interpolation is a low-level computer vision task requiring only a basic understanding of motions and the general shape of objects. Thus, the data diversity of the list is believed to be sufficient. Tab X1 reports results on the (full) LAVIB test set when training FLAVR on 700 videos from queries containing only either $\texttt{Seoul}$, $\texttt{London}$, or $\texttt{Istanbul}$.

- __Potential improvements__. From Tab. X1, specific location terms do not show a significant impact on performance. However, including more locations can potentially further increase the variance of some statistics; e.g. ARMS. In addition to weather queries, other terms such as time of day can be added to explicitly enforce diversification in the returned videos.




### Activities

- __Motivation__. As discussed in A1, activity terms are added to avoid static scenes. The distinction between sports and actions subgroups is done to control the expected motion intensity. Activities do however provide a strong constraint for the video content.


- __Remedy used__. In total, approximately \~30\% of the queries include actions. The majority of videos returned are either one-shot tours of locations or vlogs. Both types can easily be segmented into 10-second and 1-second clips by the pipeline as they include little to no edits/cuts. Sports are included in a small portion of the queries (\~4%) to avoid specialization. Table X2 ablates on 1,000 train videos sourced from queries that include different portions of activity terms. The evaluation is done on the (full) LAVIB test set. The partial inclusion of actions (30\% and 60\%) is shown to be the most balanced strategy for diversity.    


- __Limitations__. Action terms such as $\texttt{walking}$ or $\texttt{car ride}$ are generic and return a large number of videos. Despite viewpoints from hand-held or mounted cameras being some of the most common in online videos, limitations exist. 


- __Potential improvements__. The videos returned using only location are primarily compilations/highlights from aerial, bird's eye, long shot, or panoramic footages. Driving videos are also ideal for capturing overhead shots. Although both help reduce viewpoint bias, adding an additional vocabulary term based on viewpoint can increase diversity further.  



### Misc and camera types

- __Motivation__. Miscellaneous search terms were manually added to diversify the search. The returned videos can vary from the rest of LAVIB by different luminance fluctuations; e.g. $\{\texttt{underwater}\}$, low; e.g. $\{\texttt{metro}\}$ or high; e.g. $\{\texttt{birds},\texttt{flowers},\texttt{insects}\}$ contrast. 19 camera types are also selected manually to include a variety of phone cameras, action and digital cameras, and DSLRs. The difference in ARL and ALV distributions for misc and camera-based queries compared to the entire LAVIB is shown in Figs X2 and X3.


- __Remedy used__. As noted in A1, camera terms are added to \~10\% of the queries to avoid returning irrelevant videos. This was done after manually checking the video titles. Approximately 7\% of the dataset is collected with misc terms. Tab. X3 reports performance on 1,000 train examples that are partially sourced from misc queries. Similarly to Tab. X2, maintaining a balance between misc and non-misc queries improves generalizability.


- __Limitations__. The inclusion of misc terms aims to improve diversity. However, as noted, video themes such as screen captures do not guarantee significant variations in video statistics. Similarly, some camera types may not necessarily differ in video quality.


- __Potential improvements__. A further analysis on the misc queries that source videos with the most diverse statistics can highlight the specific terms that improve variance. This can also be used to weigh each term during selection. The same approach can also be applied to the camera types.

review.value:
Strengths
1. By providing a large-scale benchmark and a complete set of quantitative metrics, this paper makes significant progress in the field of video interpolation and fills a gap in existing datasets.
2. The LAVIB dataset was constructed with a complete process (including data sourcing, analysis, selection, and processing) while maintaining the large scale and diversity of the dataset.
3. This paper provides a detailed comparison of LAVIB with other existing datasets in the field and analyzes the unique challenges and contributions of LAVIB.
4. This paper take care to address potential limitations and ethical issues, thus increasing the transparency and reliability of the dataset.

Weakness
1. Although the paper mentions the computational costs of running the experiment multiple times, it does not go into detail on how to mitigate or manage these costs.
2. This paper does not discuss possible biases in the dataset as the video source is primarily web-based.
3. This paper should explain in more detail how metrics such as motion amplitude, brightness, frame sharpness, and contrast are calculated and how these metrics affect the creation of the dataset segmentation.

summary_and_contributions.value: The paper introduces LAVIB, a comprehensive dataset for video frame interpolation (VFI). LAVIB includes a large collection of high-resolution videos sourced from the web, covering diverse motion, luminance, sharpness, and contrast. It addresses the limitations of existing datasets by emphasizing quantitative analysis of video attributes. LAVIB consists of 283K clips from 17K ultra-HD videos, with train, val, and test sets maintaining similar metric distributions. It also provides out-of-distribution splits for evaluating generalization. LAVIB fills a gap in VFI datasets, offering researchers a valuable benchmark for advancing the field.

review.value: The paper is well-written. See ”Strengths" and "Opportunities For Improvement" for pros and cons.

strengths.value:
- The paper addresses the need for larger datasets in the field of video frame interpolation (VFI). By introducing LAVIB, a dataset comprising 283K clips from 17K ultra-HD videos, the authors aim to enhance the scale of available data. This larger dataset offers researchers a more extensive resource for training and evaluating VFI algorithms.
- LAVIB stands out by providing a diverse range of video attributes, including motion, luminance, sharpness, and contrast.
- The paper presents empirical evidence to support the effectiveness of LAVIB. By conducting experiments using the dataset, the authors demonstrate that the utilization of LAVIB leads to improvements in video frame interpolation.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
- While the paper claims to introduce a "large-scale" dataset, the inclusion of only 283K video clips may not fully justify this claim.
- The paper does not thoroughly discuss how bias in data collection, particularly in search terms, was minimized. Without addressing this issue, the dataset may inadvertently contain biases that could influence the performance of VFI algorithms. 
- While the paper focuses on four key dimensions (motion, luminance, sharpness, and contrast), it overlooks the impact of other crucial factors on video frame interpolation, such as resolution and frame rate (fps). Understanding how these factors affect VFI performance would provide a more comprehensive evaluation of algorithms and enable insights into their behavior across a broader range of scenarios.
- The author did not provide any video results in supplementary material or the paper page.

limitations.value: Further discussions on reducing data biases are encouraged.

documentation.value: The dataset and processing pipeline are open-source and well-documented.

ethics.value: Seems good. I don't see any major concerns here.

summary_and_contributions.value:
The paper presents LAVIB, a large-scale video interpolation benchmark with 283K clips from 17K ultra-HD videos. It introduces automated video sourcing and metrics for motion, luminance, sharpness, and contrast. LAVIB also offers both in-distribution and out-of-distribution challenge sets to evaluate video interpolation performance under diverse conditions. The contributions are as the following:
1. A large-scale high quality dataset for video interpolation
2. A good data sourcing and filtering pipeline specifically for video interpolation task
3. New trained video interpolation models based on the dataset and justify the effectiveness of the proposed dataset

review.value: The overall quality of this paper is very good, all the assumptions are well addressed and each step in collecting the dataset are clearly introduced. Experiments are sufficient, and the dataset has been already opensourced. Video interpolation would be a crucial task in current video generation research, and I believe this dataset has significance meaning to the research community since many video-related tasks such as video generation cannot support high fps now.

strengths.value:
- Writing is good an clear.
- Statistics of the dataset is sufficient.
- Well-designed metrics to compare with previous dataset
- Clear presenting every step of building this dataset and all the parameters used in each step
- Experiments are sufficient to show the effectiveness of this dataset

opportunities_for_improvement.value: The proposed dataset has narrow distribution from the query used to scrape the dataset, and all the videos are realistic style. More videos in other domain such as anime or 3D rendering would significantly increase the usefulness of this dataset. I'd encourage the author to enhance the dataset with wider distribution.

limitations.value: Limitations and societal impact are well-addressed.

relation_to_prior_work.value: Yes, the relation to prior work is clearly discussed.

documentation.value: I don't find documentation and intended uses in the dataset website, the availability and maintenance are also missing. I encourage the author to complete these parts.

title.value: LAVIB: A Large-scale Video Interpolation Benchmark

abstract.value: This paper introduces a LArge-scale Video Interpolation Benchmark (LAVIB) for the low-level video task of Video Frame Interpolation (VFI). LAVIB comprises a large collection of high-resolution videos sourced from the web through an automated pipeline with minimal requirements for human verification. Metrics are computed for each video's motion magnitudes, luminance conditions, frame sharpness, and contrast. The collection of videos and the creation of quantitative challenges based on these metrics are under-explored by current low-level video task datasets. In total, LAVIB includes 283K clips from 17K ultra-HD videos, covering 77.6 hours. Benchmark train, val, and test sets maintain similar video metric distributions. Further splits are also created for out-of-distribution (OOD) challenges, with train and test splits including videos of dissimilar attributes.

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
